mcq.q: The model knows the policy but formats answers wrongly despite examples. Try…
options: Continued pretraining on policy text
RAG over the policy documents
SFT (often LoRA)
A larger context window for more examples
mcq.why: Behaviour/format gaps are what supervised fine-tuning addresses.
distractors: The model already knows the policy; this is a behaviour gap.
Retrieval supplies facts, which are not missing.
Examples already failed to fix the format.

mcq.q: What is the rule for moving up the adaptation ladder?
options: Start with fine-tuning to get the best result early
Move up only when evaluation shows the current rung falls short
Always try continued pretraining as the first step
Move up whenever a new model version is released
mcq.why: Each rung roughly multiplies cost, data needs and maintenance.
distractors: Fine-tuning is costly; cheaper rungs often suffice.
That is the most expensive rung.
Releases are not evidence of a gap.

mcq.q: Answers contain wrong or outdated facts with no citations. What is the likely remedy?
options: Retrieval
Distillation
Continued pretraining
Fine-tuning
mcq.why: Missing or changing facts are a retrieval problem (9.1).
distractors: Too costly and still freezes facts.
Fine-tuning changes behaviour and freezes facts.

mcq.q: A large model does the task well but is too slow and expensive at your volume. What fits?
options: Retrieval of more context
Distilling into a small model
A longer, more detailed prompt
Continued pretraining on the task
mcq.why: Generate verified teacher outputs on real inputs and fine-tune a small student.
distractors: Far more costly, and not the gap.

mcq.q: Distillation example: 3 million items a month at $0.004 each. What is the monthly cost?
Before distilling from a large model, what must you check?
options: That the teacher's licence permits it
That the teacher model is open source
That the student model is larger
That no human checks the teacher's outputs
mcq.why: Some licences restrict using outputs to train other models.

mcq.q: When is continued pretraining justified?
options: When the facts the assistant needs change every single week
When domain language is far from general text and data is huge
When answers keep coming out in the wrong format or style
When the cost per call is too high at the volume you serve
mcq.why: It is costly and needs SFT afterwards to restore instruction following.

mcq.q: A prompt needs 4,000 tokens of rules on every call. What does the chapter suggest?
options: Add more rules to cover the gaps
Use retrieval to fetch the rules
Continued pretraining on the rules
Fine-tune the rules in; keep a short prompt
mcq.why: Fine-tuning can move stable behaviour into the model and cut prompt tokens.
distractors: Rules are behaviour, needed on every call.

mcq.q: Retrieval misses domain synonyms and codes. What is the likely remedy?
options: Use a bigger LLM to write answers
Fine-tune the embedder or reranker
Fine-tune the LLM on domain answers
Distil the LLM into a smaller one
mcq.why: The miss is in the retriever, so adapt the retriever (13.5).
distractors: The LLM never sees the missed passages.

mcq.q: In the distillation case, the student was 1 point less accurate. Why was it accepted?
options: The teacher model had been wrong all along
The drop was not on critical exception types
Accuracy does not matter for this task
The student was right on all new data
mcq.why: An average drop is acceptable only if critical segments are not hurt.
distractors: It matters; the drop was checked.

mcq.q: An assistant gets last week's price changes wrong but answers in the right format and tone. Which rung of the ladder addresses this?
options: Fine-tuning on the new price list
Distilling into a smaller, cheaper model
Continued pretraining on price documents
Retrieval of the current prices at question time
mcq.why: Missing or changing facts are a retrieval gap; fine-tuning would go stale again.
distractors: Prices change; the weights would be stale again.
Far too costly for changing facts.

mcq.q: Illustratively, a hosted teacher costs $0.012 per request and a distilled self-hosted student $0.0015. At 2 million requests a month, roughly how much does distillation save each month?
options: About $24,000
About $3,000
About $21,000
About $2,100
mcq.why: (0.012 − 0.0015) × 2,000,000 = $21,000, before the cost of building and evaluating the student.
distractors: That is the teacher's whole cost, ignoring the student's.
That is the student's cost, not the saving.
That drops a factor of ten.

mcq.q: LoRA trainable parameters for one 4096×4096 matrix at rank 8?
distractors: 8,192 is d_in + d_out, before multiplying by the rank 8.
4,096 is one dimension, not the parameter count.

mcq.q: What does LoRA train?
options: Two small matrices B and A added to a frozen W
Only the embedding layer of the model
A new tokenizer for the domain
All weights of the model at once
mcq.why: The layer computes W·x + (α/r)·B·A·x with W frozen.
distractors: LoRA adapts weight matrices inside layers.

mcq.q: LoRA trainable parameters for a 4096 × 14,336 matrix at rank 8?
About how much training memory does full fine-tuning with mixed-precision Adam need per parameter?
options: About 64 bytes
About 2 bytes
About 16 bytes
About 0.5 bytes
mcq.why: Weights, gradients and optimiser state add up to about 16 bytes per parameter (6.6).

mcq.q: Using 16 bytes per parameter, about how much memory does full fine-tuning of an 8B model need?
options: About 1 TB
About 16 GB
About 32 GB
About 128 GB
mcq.why: 8 × 10⁹ × 16 bytes ≈ 128 GB, before activations.
distractors: That is roughly BF16 weights only.

mcq.q: What does QLoRA change compared with LoRA?
options: The frozen base is 4-bit (NF4); adapters train in higher precision
It removes the adapters and trains the base model directly
The adapters are trained in 4-bit precision on a BF16 base
The base model is unfrozen and quantised to 4-bit while training
mcq.why: This lets large models fit on a single GPU, at some speed cost.
distractors: The base is 4-bit; adapters are not.

mcq.q: After training, what can you do with B·A?
options: Nothing; it must stay a separate file
Retrain the base model with it
Only discard it after evaluation
Merge it into W, or keep it as an adapter
mcq.why: Both options are available.

mcq.q: Where does most of LoRA's memory saving come from?
options: Gradients are not computed at all
Optimiser state only for A and B
Activations no longer need memory
The base model is deleted after loading
mcq.why: The frozen base needs no optimiser state or weight gradients.

mcq.q: Few trainable parameters means low compute. True?
options: Only on CPUs, where compute is cheaper
No: the base still runs forward and backward
Yes, always, with any kind of adapter
Yes, as long as QLoRA is the method used
mcq.why: Compute scales with the full model's forward and backward passes.

mcq.q: In the LoRA calculator, how does moving from q, v to all linear modules at the same rank change the trainable parameters?
options: It decreases them, as ranks are shared
It doubles the rank of each adapter
It increases them: more matrices get adapters
No change, since the rank is the same
mcq.why: Parameters are summed over targeted matrices; all linear includes the large MLP matrices.
distractors: Each matrix gets its own adapter.

mcq.q: LoRA at rank 16 targets q (4096 → 4096) and v (4096 → 1024) in all 32 layers of an 8B-shaped model. Roughly how many trainable parameters is that?
options: About 8.4M
About 0.2M
About 6.8M
About 3.4M
distractors: That treats v as 4096 × 4096; with 8 KV heads it is 1024 wide.

mcq.q: A team has one 24 GB GPU and wants to fine-tune an 8B model for a format task. Which approach fits?
options: QLoRA: a 4-bit base with LoRA adapters
LoRA on a BF16 base with a large batch
Continued pretraining on the whole model
Full fine-tuning in mixed precision
mcq.why: QLoRA on an 8B model fits a single 16–24 GB GPU.
distractors: Tight at best, and large batches add activation memory.
Costly, and the wrong rung for a format task.
That needs about 16 bytes per parameter, far beyond 24 GB.

mcq.q: After fine-tuning, multilingual accuracy fell 7 points. You should…
options: Ship, since the domain score improved
Treat it as a failed gate; retrain with mixed data
Ignore it; non-English traffic is small
Lower the temperature and re-test
mcq.why: General-capability regressions are release blockers when they breach the gate.
distractors: It is a regression for those users.

mcq.q: What is the honest baseline for measuring domain gains?
options: The previous fine-tune only
The base model with your best prompt
The base model with a weak prompt
A random-guess baseline
mcq.why: A weak baseline exaggerates the gain.
distractors: Far too weak to be honest.

mcq.q: What is catastrophic forgetting?
options: A training run that failed partway
Forgetting the training data itself
Losing the adapter file on disk
Losing general skills after fine-tuning
mcq.why: Run general suites before and after; LoRA forgets less, but not nothing.

mcq.q: How can you test for memorisation?
options: Prefix probes for verbatim completions, plus planted canaries
Check that the final training loss is not too low
Measure latency on long prompts built from training data
Ask the model directly whether it memorised any records
mcq.why: Probes and canaries test extraction.

mcq.q: Can fine-tuning on benign data weaken refusal behaviour?
options: Only for full fine-tuning, not LoRA
Only for small models, not large ones
Yes; rerun safety suites on every model
No, only harmful data does that
mcq.why: Safety regressions are a known effect of fine-tuning.

mcq.q: In the scorecard, which gates fail?
options: Multilingual and refusal
Domain extraction and canaries
Instruction following and fabrication
None of the six gates fail
mcq.why: Multilingual fell 7.3 points (limit 3) and refusal fell to 91.5% (gate 97%).

mcq.q: General instruction following fell from 81.0% to 78.5%. With a gate of “drop ≤ 3 points”, does it pass?
options: Cannot tell from these numbers
Yes: a 2.5-point drop
No; it fell below 80%
No; any drop at all fails
distractors: The gate is a drop, not a floor.

mcq.q: Two gates fail on the scorecard. What does the chapter recommend?
options: Add those examples to the mix and retrain
Ship it and monitor the gaps
Lower the two failing gates
Ship to English users only, quietly
mcq.why: Fix the regressions, do not ship and hope.
distractors: Hiding a regression is not a fix.

mcq.q: A few privacy probes find nothing. What does that prove?
options: That no data can be extracted at all
That canaries are not needed next time
That it is safe to release with PII
Only that those probes found nothing
mcq.why: Absence of evidence from a few probes is weak; minimise PII in training data in the first place.
distractors: Absence of evidence is not proof.

mcq.q: An adapter raises average field accuracy but begins inventing plausible IDs for missing fields. What should happen?
options: Remove the fabrication test from the suite
Block release: the fabrication gate wins
Lower the fabrication gate to let it pass
Ship, since the average accuracy improved
mcq.why: A higher average does not excuse a critical failure mode.

mcq.q: A fine-tuned model scores 8 points above the base model with a weak prompt, but only 1 point above the base model with the team's best prompt. What should the report say?
options: The gain is 4.5 points, the average of the two
The gain is 8 points, since that is the measured difference
The real gain is about 1 point, against the best-prompt baseline
There is no gain, since prompting works almost as well
mcq.why: The honest baseline is the base model with your best prompt.
distractors: Averaging does not make a baseline honest.
A weak prompt flatters the fine-tune.
One point may matter; report it honestly.

mcq.q: Which tends to produce a better fine-tuned model?
options: Tens of thousands of noisy examples
Only synthetic data
A few thousand consistent examples
Any data, as long as there is a lot
mcq.why: The model learns whatever the data shows, including inconsistency.

mcq.q: What should a labelling guideline include?
options: Only the output schema that each label has to fill in
The model's system prompt for the task, copied as it is
Task, schema, rules, examples, edge cases and what to do if unsure
Only a set of worked examples, without written rules
mcq.why: A versioned guideline makes labels consistent.
distractors: Rules and edge cases are needed too.

mcq.q: Two annotators have low agreement on a pilot. What should you fix first?
options: The annotators
The guideline
The model
Nothing; average their labels
mcq.why: Low agreement points to unclear rules.
distractors: Fix the guideline, not the annotators.

mcq.q: Observed agreement is 0.90 and agreement expected by chance is 0.50. What is Cohen's kappa?
distractors: That is po − pe without dividing.

mcq.q: One annotator accepted 99% of model drafts unchanged while others edited 22%. What is the likely problem?
options: The model is perfect
That annotator is the most skilled
The other annotators are too strict
Rubber-stamping
mcq.why: Their accepted records had three times the error rate.
distractors: The others found errors to fix.
Higher acceptance came with more errors.

mcq.q: How did the team in the example detect rubber-stamping in future?
options: Fired the annotator who accepted drafts
Raised the acceptance target for drafts
Stopped using model drafts altogether
Hid the draft on 10% of items (blind check)
mcq.why: Blind items show whether an annotator really reads.
distractors: Firing does not detect future cases.
Drafts are useful; they need checks.

mcq.q: When should the test set be split off?
options: Never; test on the training data you have
First, by customer or time if leakage is possible
After training, from whatever data is left
Whenever the model looks good enough to test
mcq.why: Hold out the test set first and never train on it.

mcq.q: Choose all the automatic quality checks the chapter lists.
options: Deduplication
Contamination check against the evaluation set
Removing every hard case
Schema validity
mcq.why: Also PII scans and length or banned-content checks.
distractors: Hard cases are needed in the data.

mcq.q: What goes in a dataset's datasheet?
options: The model's accuracy when trained on it
Sources, guideline version, annotators, gaps
The annotators' names and personal details
Only the number of rows and columns
mcq.why: The datasheet documents how the data was made.
distractors: That belongs to the model card.
Never needed, and a privacy risk.
Too little to judge the data.

mcq.q: Where should inputs for a training set come from?
options: Only the easiest examples, for clean labels
Only synthetic prompts written by a model
Real, privacy-reviewed traffic, including hard cases
Public benchmarks for the same kind of task
mcq.why: Real inputs match what the model will see.
distractors: The model must learn hard cases.

mcq.q: Two annotators agree on 85% of a pilot's items, and the agreement expected by chance is 50%. What is Cohen's κ?
distractors: That is raw agreement, not corrected for chance.
That is the numerator only, not divided by (1 − chance).

mcq.q: Annotators accept 99% of model-drafted labels without edits, but a blind check finds many of those labels wrong. What is happening, and what helps?
options: The guideline is perfect, so annotators have nothing to add
Rubber-stamping: track edit rates and keep blind checks
Annotators need faster tools to keep up with the drafts
The model is excellent, so remove the human review step
mcq.why: Model drafts speed work, but annotators can stop reading; edit rates and blind items reveal it.
distractors: Low edits plus errors point to inattention.
The blind check shows the drafts are often wrong.

mcq.q: In extraction training data, why include many examples where a field is absent?
options: Because absent fields are easier to label
Otherwise it learns to always fill fields
To make the training set smaller
To make extraction run faster
mcq.why: Without null examples, the model fabricates values.

mcq.q: In the contract example, only 2% of training examples had the termination clause absent. What happened?
options: The model ignored the clause entirely
It invented a clause 31% of the time
Accuracy dropped to 50% across fields
Nothing; 2% was plenty of examples
mcq.why: Adding 600 absent-field examples brought fabrication to 2%.

mcq.q: For classification, what is often cheaper and as good as an LLM?
options: A larger LLM with better prompts
Continued pretraining on labels
A longer prompt with more classes
A small fine-tuned encoder
mcq.why: Small encoders classify well at a fraction of the cost.

mcq.q: Which domain-language adaptation has the highest regression risk?
options: Continued pretraining, then SFT
Constrained decoding of the output
Few-shot prompting with domain terms
Retrieval over domain documents
mcq.why: Mix in general data (e.g. 10–30%) to reduce forgetting.

mcq.q: When might constrained decoding be enough without training?
options: For calibrating classification scores
For deciding when to call a tool
For learning domain vocabulary
For output in an exact format
mcq.why: Constrained decoding (7.4) enforces the schema at generation time.

mcq.q: Why do tool-use training records include the tool result turn?
options: To hide the tool output from the model
So it learns to use results, not just call tools
Because every chat template requires it
To make the records longer for training
mcq.why: The model must learn the whole loop.

mcq.q: Choose all the evaluation measures listed for extraction.
options: Perplexity on general text
Hallucinated-field rate
Field-level exact match
Null accuracy
mcq.why: Perplexity is for domain language, not extraction.
distractors: Listed for domain language, not extraction.

mcq.q: After tool-use fine-tuning, the assistant calls search_orders even when a user just writes “thanks, bye”. What was missing from the training data?
options: Only failed calls
Random tool calls
Only the final answer
“No tool needed” cases
mcq.why: Otherwise the model learns to call tools for everything.
distractors: Failures alone teach the wrong thing.
The calls and results matter too.

mcq.q: A fine-tuned model produces valid tool calls in the right format. Does that authorise execution?
options: Yes, if the model's confidence is high
Only for read-only tools, not writes
No: authorisation and policy still apply
Yes, since a valid format proves intent
mcq.why: Training shapes behaviour; the runtime still checks every call (11.3).

mcq.q: Which chat template should tool-use fine-tuning use?
options: Plain text with no role markers
The template of a different model
The model's own tool-calling template
Any custom template the team likes
mcq.why: Matching the native template keeps the format the model and serving stack expect.
distractors: The model was trained with roles.

mcq.q: An extraction training set has 30,000 records, 600 of them with the field absent (2%). Roughly how many absent-field examples must you add for absent cases to make up 10% of the set?
options: About 2,700
About 2,400
About 600
About 3,000
distractors: That forgets that the set grows as you add examples.
That only doubles the share to about 4%.
That is 10% of the original 30,000, not the number to add.

mcq.q: A team needs output in an exact house JSON format. The model gets the content right, and the team has few labelled examples. What should it try first?
options: A larger model with a longer prompt full of rules
Full fine-tuning on the few examples the team has
Constrained decoding against the schema, before any fine-tuning
Continued pretraining on a large set of JSON documents
mcq.why: When only the format is wrong, constrained decoding may be enough without training.
distractors: That adds cost without enforcing the format.
Few examples risk overfitting, and training may be unnecessary.
Far too costly for a format gap.

mcq.q: Why is fine-tuning the retriever often the highest-return adaptation in a RAG system?
options: Embedders miss domain meaning, and tuning them is cheap
Retrievers never need to be evaluated afterwards
It removes the need for a reranker in the pipeline
LLMs cannot be fine-tuned for retrieval tasks at all
mcq.why: Codenames, part numbers and terms of art are common misses.
distractors: They need it like anything else.

mcq.q: What are hard negatives?
options: Duplicate copies of the positive passage
Queries in the logs that have no answer
Near-misses mined from the current model's top results
Random passages drawn from across the corpus
mcq.why: They teach fine distinctions and matter more than more easy pairs.

mcq.q: Why is a new reranker an easier first step than a new embedding model?
options: Embedding models cannot be fine-tuned at all
Rerankers are always more accurate than embedders
Rerankers need no labelled training data
A reranker needs no re-index; a new embedder does
mcq.why: Re-embedding means a blue/green migration (10.7).

mcq.q: Which loss is typical for embedding fine-tuning?
options: Cross-entropy over the vocabulary
Mean squared error on token IDs
Contrastive loss with in-batch negatives
Hinge loss on class labels
mcq.why: It pulls queries and positives together and pushes negatives apart (4.4).

mcq.q: Where should you evaluate a fine-tuned retriever?
options: On a general benchmark only
On real labelled queries, not synthetic ones
On the synthetic training queries
On the training passages themselves
mcq.why: Synthetic training queries overstate gains.
distractors: It may not reflect your domain.

mcq.q: A mined hard negative is actually a valid answer. What happens if you train on it?
options: Nothing changes in the model
It learns to reject good evidence
Recall improves on those queries
The index shrinks in size
mcq.why: Check mined negatives before training.
distractors: Training does not change the index size.

mcq.q: In the synthetic pipeline, why filter generated questions?
options: To make the generated questions shorter
To speed up the training runs that follow
To drop questions the chunk cannot answer
To remove typos from the generated questions
mcq.why: A judge or round-trip check removes bad pairs.

mcq.q: A team wants to fine-tune its retriever but has no labelled (query, passage) pairs. Which of these could supply them? Choose all that apply.
options: Random pairs from the corpus
LLM-generated questions per chunk, filtered
FAQ structures
Search logs with clicked or used results
mcq.why: Human labelling is another source.
distractors: Random pairs are not relevant pairs.

mcq.q: After fine-tuning embeddings for jargon, what should you also check?
options: Only the final training loss
Nothing else; jargon is the goal
Regressions on general queries
Only the size of the new index
mcq.why: Gains on jargon can come with losses elsewhere.

mcq.q: How are rerankers (cross-encoders) typically trained?
options: With unlabelled domain text only
By clustering passages by topic
With next-token prediction on text
As classifiers over query–passage pairs
mcq.why: They score each query–passage pair.

mcq.q: A fine-tuned retriever reaches Recall@10 of 0.95 on its synthetic questions but 0.71 on real labelled user queries. What should the team conclude?
options: Average the two and report 0.83 as the retriever's recall
The real-query score is the true measure; the synthetic set flatters it
Train longer on the synthetic set until real recall catches up
The real queries must be mislabelled, since synthetic recall is high
mcq.why: Evaluate on real human queries, not on synthetic ones like those you trained on.
distractors: An average hides the real gap.
That fits the synthetic style even more.

mcq.q: Embeddings miss internal codenames such as “Project Kestrel”, but the team cannot afford a full re-index this quarter. What is the sensible first step?
options: Fine-tune the embedder and swap it in place today
Remove codenames from the documents
Fine-tune a reranker, which needs no re-index
Fine-tune the answer LLM on codenames
mcq.why: A reranker re-scores candidates without touching the index; a new embedder needs a full re-index.
distractors: A new embedder needs a full blue/green re-index.
That loses meaning users search for.
The LLM never sees the missed passages.

Only the final accuracy number on the validation set
Config, commit, data and base versions, hyperparameters, metrics, artefacts
The annotators' names and the shifts they worked on the data

mcq.q: Why is exact bitwise reproduction often impossible on GPUs?
options: GPUs lose some data between training steps
Python itself is not a deterministic language
GPU kernels vary; aim for metrics within tolerance
Random seeds do not work at all on GPUs
mcq.why: Pin environments and seeds, record hardware, and compare within tolerance.
distractors: The non-determinism is in GPU kernels.
Seeds help; some kernels still vary.

mcq.q: What does a model registry provide?
options: Training compute for each team
A tokenizer for each model
Immutable versions and stages
Annotation tools for datasets
mcq.why: Each version is traceable to its data and code.

mcq.q: Choose all the release criteria the chapter lists.
options: Approval by an owner and a rollback plan
A model card
The highest score on any benchmark
Pre-agreed gates
mcq.why: Release needs gates, documentation, approval and a way back.
distractors: A single benchmark score is not a release criterion.

mcq.q: What goes in a model card?
options: Intended use, data summary, evaluation, limits, licence
Only the model's name, version and owner
The full training code and its config files
Only the GPU type and hours used for training
mcq.why: It documents what the model is for and how it performed.

mcq.q: An adapter was tested on base revision A. Can it be deployed on base revision B without re-testing?
options: No: a new base needs re-testing
Yes, if the base names match
Yes, adapters are portable
Only if revision B is newer
mcq.why: The adapter's behaviour depends on the exact base weights.
distractors: Names can point to new weights.
They are tied to the base weights.

options: DVC, lakeFS or HF dataset revisions
Label Studio annotation projects
The MLflow model registry only
TRL training scripts and configs

options: Registries require numeric IDs
Names are too long to store
Names can point to new weights
Revisions are faster to load

mcq.q: A fine-tuned model was promoted to production on Monday. On Wednesday it shows a regression. What should have happened to the previous version at promotion?
options: Be renamed to the new version
Be retrained
Be deleted
Stay available for rollback

options: The operating system's name
The Python version number
The image tag “latest”
The image digest

mcq.q: Six months after launch, an auditor asks which data trained the production model. The team only knows it is called “support-model-final”. What was missing?
options: A larger GPU for the training run so it is easier to repeat
Keeping a copy of the training data in the model's folder
A registry of immutable versions linked to the run and dataset version
A longer and more descriptive model name with the date in it
mcq.why: Lineage traces a model version to exactly the data and code that made it.
distractors: Files without versions and links do not prove lineage.
Names do not identify weights or data.

mcq.q: Rerunning a fine-tuning job with the same config, data and seed gives an accuracy 0.3 points different on the same test set. What does the chapter say?
options: The seed was ignored, so seeds should be removed
The dataset must have changed silently between runs
The run is broken and must be debugged until bitwise equal
Expected: aim for the same metrics within tolerance, not bitwise equality
mcq.why: Non-deterministic GPU operations make exact reproduction hard.
distractors: Seeds help; some kernels still vary.
A small difference is expected with fixed data.
Bitwise equality is often impossible on GPUs.
